# @webwriter/lit

> [!NPM]
>
> [View `@webwriter/lit` on npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@webwriter/lit)

`@webwriter/lit` supplies a Lit base class for widgets. It also supplies signal helpers and a standalone drawer for embedded widgets.

## `LitElementWw`

Import `LitElementWw` from `@webwriter/lit`. Call `super` when you override a [lifecycle callback](https://lit.dev/docs/components/lifecycle/).

| Member | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `standalone` | The reflected attribute value. Its value is `null` when the attribute is absent. Render a [standalone widget drawer](#standalone-widget-drawer) to show the controls. |
| `editable` | Getter for `isContentEditable`. Updates when the widget or an ancestor changes editing mode. |
| `lang` | The reactive language. Without an explicit value, it uses the language from the nearest ancestor that sets it. |
| `static scopedElements` | Maps tag names to component classes. All instances of the same widget class share its native registry. |
| `registry` | The widget class's native `CustomElementRegistry`. |
| `static properties` | Lit [reactive property](https://lit.dev/docs/components/properties/) declarations. Declare option metadata separately. |
| `static options` / `static actions` | Default widget drawer declarations. Use instance getters `get options()` and `get actions()` for declarations that depend on widget state. |
| `static signals` / `static effects`, `signals` / `effects` | Declare what the widget publishes and receives. `static signals` maps a signal name to its `shape`, `label` and `description`. `static effects` maps an effect attribute to `connect`, `label`, `description` and `accepts`. The instance `signals` object holds the read-only signals. See [Signals](#signals). |
| `widgetRuntime` | The widget's public `WidgetRuntime` instance, shared with its language and data hooks. |
| `localize` | Optional `{getLocale, setLocale}` connection from [`@lit/localize`](https://lit.dev/docs/localization/overview/). |
| `static dataType` | Default MIME type for an inert data block. The initial value is undefined. |
| `dataType` | Type of the current data block. It uses the class default when necessary. |
| `data` | Raw text of the direct scoped data block. Without a scoped block, it uses the first direct inert script child that has no `src`. The value is `null` when no block exists. A write uses `dataType` or `text/plain`. |
| `setData(type, value, attrs?)` | Creates a block or updates the current block. An update keeps the block's identity and attributes. The method rejects executable types, `src`, and unsafe closing script tags. It escapes `<` characters in JSON. |
| `dataReady` | Indicates that the current data scope accepts writes. |
| `dataPending(context)` | Override to show that a participant scope is loading. |
| `dataChanged(text, context)` | Override to read initial, accepted local, remote, and undo or redo snapshots. Update the display without writing data. |
| `dataError(error, context)` | Override to display a connection or data validation error. |

Data hooks receive raw text and a `{block, mode}` context. Modes are `individual`, `all`, `group`, or `local`. Override these hooks to respond to changes in the data block. The base class requests the current state on connection. This also applies to late custom element upgrades. The hooks apply only to the widget's own data block.

A write through `data` or `setData()` throws `InvalidStateError` while a managed scope is pending. After a validation error on a ready scope, the widget can try a corrected write.

For scoped data, use a [data block](../domeditor/docs/widgets/reference/data.md) with JSON or XML and `slot="data"`. Set `sharedData: true` in the editing configuration. The authoring tool supplies the scoped data connection. Outside the managed runtime, authored data stays local. The hooks use `mode: "local"`.

Changes to the data block through the DOM also cause a call to `dataChanged`. A replacement block starts a new data connection. A write through a helper keeps the current block.

The base class uses [native scoped registry APIs](../domeditor/docs/widgets/reference/runtime.md#scoped-custom-element-registries) directly.

The widget keeps an explicit `lang=""` value. When it inherits a language, it reads the value from its ancestor. A change to the effective language updates the optional localization connection. If the update fails, the widget dispatches `localizationerror` with `{error}`.

## Options and actions in Lit

Declare Lit reactive properties in `static properties`. Set fields such as `reflect`, `state`, and `converter` there.

If an option has no `attribute`, the authoring tool uses the attribute name from the matching Lit property declaration. A property with `attribute: false` or `state: true` has no option attribute by default.

Replace legacy `option` and `action` decorators with `static options` and `static actions`. Use `static optionGroups` for group declarations. The authoring tool records the DOM changes from an action as one undo step. The drawer ignores `placeholder` in a Lit action declaration. [Options and actions](../domeditor/docs/widgets/reference/options-actions.md) describes the interface.

## Conversions in Lit

`LitElementWw` types `static convertFrom` and `static convertTo`, and the instance members `convertFrom` and `convertTo`. An instance member has priority over the static map. A key that starts with a dot, such as `.json`, or holds a slash, such as `image/png`, declares a file format. Every other key is the lowercase tag of an HTML element, such as `ul`. Import and export handlers take the widget as `this` and are given by method name or as functions.

```ts
import {LitElementWw, type ConvertFromDeclarations, type ConvertToDeclarations} from "@webwriter/lit"

class WwPackingList extends LitElementWw {
  static convertFrom = {
    ul: "loadList",
    ".json": "importJson",
  } satisfies ConvertFromDeclarations<WwPackingList>

  static convertTo = {
    ul: "toList",
    "text/plain": "exportText",
  } satisfies ConvertToDeclarations<WwPackingList>

  loadList(fragment: DocumentFragment) { this.replaceChildren(fragment) }
  async importJson(file: File) {
    if(file.size > 1024 * 1024) throw new Error("The file is larger than 1 MiB.") // Localize the text with msg()
    const items: string[] = JSON.parse(await file.text())
    return () => this.replaceChildren(...items.map(text => Object.assign(document.createElement("li"), {textContent: text})))
  }
  toList() { return this.querySelector(":scope > ul")?.cloneNode(true) as Element | null }
  exportText() { return new File([this.textContent ?? ""], "list.txt", {type: "text/plain"}) }
}
```

`satisfies` checks each handler against the kind of its key. A file key rejects a handler that returns an element, and a handler of a tag key must not return a `File`. Without `satisfies`, a plain `static convertFrom = {...}` is checked against the base class when the class is declared. Annotate the parameters of handlers that you write inline, such as `(file: File) => ...`. The types are `ConvertFromDeclarations`, `ConvertToDeclarations`, `ElementImportHandler`, `FileImportHandler`, `FileImportResult`, `ElementExportHandler`, `FileExportHandler`, `FileExtensionKey`, `MediaTypeKey`, and `FileFormatKey`. The [conversion guide](../domeditor/docs/widgets/guides/conversions.md) explains the keys and how an import reports a bad file. The [runtime reference](../domeditor/docs/widgets/reference/runtime.md#conversions) lists the return values.

## Modules

A module supplies one common widget behavior. Import each module from its own path. A widget bundles only the modules that it imports.

Most modules are Lit [reactive controllers](https://lit.dev/docs/composition/controllers/). Create the controller in a private field. Mark elements in the shadow template with `data-ww-*` attributes. Listen for the module's `ww-*` events. The module handles pointer, touch, and keyboard input. It also handles announcements and cleanup. The examples in this section are TypeScript.

| Module | Import path | Exports | Use it to |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Permissions](#permissions) | `@webwriter/lit/permissions` | `Permissions`, `widgetPermissions`, `can`, `isEditing` | Show a control or allow an interaction only when the author grants it. |
| [Settings](#settings) | `@webwriter/lit/settings` | `Settings` | Store a setting as an attribute and edit it in the Widget drawer or in a control. |
| [Shortcuts](#shortcuts) | `@webwriter/lit/shortcuts` | `Shortcuts` | Run an action from a key. |
| [Drag](#drag) | `@webwriter/lit/drag` | `Drag` | Reorder, move, copy, or link items by pointer, keyboard, or click. |
| [Viewport](#viewport) | `@webwriter/lit/viewport` | `Viewport` | Zoom and pan a window onto larger content. |
| [Help](#help) | `@webwriter/lit/help` | `Help` | Label the controls of the widget in an overlay. |
| [Scene](#scene) | `@webwriter/lit/scene`, `@webwriter/widget/scene` | `SceneController`, `sceneElements` | Select, move, resize, and connect the elements of a drawing. Export it as SVG or an image. Print it. |
| [Print note](#print-note) | `@webwriter/lit/print` | `PrintNote`, `documentAddress` | Tell the reader on paper to open the document online. |
| [Playback](#playback) | `@webwriter/lit/playback` | `Playback` | Run steps, a simulation, or media with play, pause, and seek controls. |
| [Data block](#data-block-jsondata) | `@webwriter/lit/data` | `jsonData` | Read and write a JSON [data block](../domeditor/docs/widgets/reference/data.md). |
| [Localization](#localization-localizer-widgetmsg) | `@webwriter/lit/localize` | `localizer`, `widgetMsg` | Show the widget's own text in the document language. |
| [Exercise](#exercise) | `@webwriter/lit/exercise` | `Exercise`, `exerciseProperties`, `exerciseOptions`, `scoreOf`, `firstOrder`, `exerciseAggregate`, `obfuscated` | Build a question with a response, a solution, feedback, and form submission. |
| [Helpers](#helpers-transaction-and-whilevisible) | `@webwriter/widget/transaction`, `@webwriter/widget/visible` | `transaction`, `whileVisible` | Group a change into one undo step. Run a frame loop only while the widget is on screen. |

These rules apply to every module.

- A module option named `can` is a function. The module calls it before and during an interaction. The module cancels the interaction when the function returns false.
- A module that changes the document wraps the change and the next render in one [undo transaction](../domeditor/docs/widgets/reference/runtime.md#undo-transactions). A module with the option `rendered` waits for the render that it supplies. The binding sets it to the host's `updateComplete`.
- A module writes to the widget's shadow DOM. It writes to the host or to authored children only where its section says so. It removes its listeners, observers, timers, and adopted styles when the widget disconnects.
- Modules show and speak their own text in the widget's language. Each language loads on first use. Pass `messages` to a module to replace a text.
- Do not store a controller in a public member named `permissions`, `options`, `actions`, `data`, or `localize`. The editor reads these members as declarations. Use a private field such as `#permissions`. The widget warns in development when it finds a controller there.

### Permissions

Permissions turns each entry of `static permissions` into one answer, `can(name)`. Use it to hide controls that readers may not use and to give other modules a `can` function.

Import `Permissions` and `widgetPermissions` from `@webwriter/lit/permissions`. The module also exports the functions `can(host, name)` and `isEditing(host)`, which answer for a widget or for any element in its shadow tree without holding the controller.

| Declaration | Meaning |
|---|---|
| [`static permissions`](../domeditor/docs/widgets/reference/options-actions.md#element-permissions) | The editor's declaration. A granted permission is an empty attribute on the widget. |
| `data-ww-can="name"` | Hides the shadow element while `can(name)` is false. |
| `data-ww-can="edit"` | Shows the shadow element in edit mode only. |
| `data-ww-can-mode="disable"` | Makes the element with `data-ww-can` inert instead of hidden. |
| `editing`, `attribute` | Options of the controller. `editing` is a function that tells edit mode. `attribute` is a function that maps a permission name to its attribute. |

The controller has `can(name)` and `editing`. The widget renders again when either answer changes.

```ts
import {LitElementWw} from "@webwriter/lit"
import {Permissions} from "@webwriter/lit/permissions"
import {html, nothing} from "lit"

class WwHintCard extends LitElementWw {
  static properties = {
    allowHint: {type: Boolean, attribute: "allow-hint", reflect: true},
    open: {state: true},
  }

  static permissions = {
    allowHint: {label: {_: "Learners may reveal the hint in this widget"}},
  }

  declare allowHint: boolean
  declare open: boolean

  #permissions = new Permissions(this)

  constructor() {
    super()
    this.allowHint = false
    this.open = false
  }

  render() {
    return html`
      <slot></slot>
      <button data-ww-can="allowHint" @click=${() => (this.open = !this.open)}>Hint</button>
      <button data-ww-can="edit" @click=${() => this.querySelector("[slot=hint]")?.remove()}>Remove hint</button>
      ${this.open && this.#permissions.can("allowHint") ? html`<slot name="hint"></slot>` : nothing}
    `
  }
}

customElements.define("ww-hint-card", WwHintCard)
```

- `can(name)` is true in edit mode. In read mode it is true while the permission's attribute is on the widget. A name that the widget does not declare is refused in read mode, also when an attribute of that name is present.
- `edit` is reserved for controls that only authors see. No permission can have this name. `can("edit")` is true in edit mode only.
- The attribute comes from `attribute` in the declaration, then from the Lit property of the same name, then from the lowercase name.
- Edit mode is the `contenteditable` state that the authoring tool sets on the widget. The answers follow every change of that state and of the permission attributes, also from undo and from other participants.
- The module sets `hidden` or `inert` on shadow elements. Its style sheet makes `hidden` win over any `display` rule. It writes nothing to the authored DOM.
- A component inside the widget's shadow tree has no editing state of its own. Create `#permissions = widgetPermissions(this)` in it. The component then answers like the surrounding widget and renders again when the answers change. A component that also marks elements with `data-ww-can` creates `new Permissions(this)`, which follows the widget in the same way.
- A running interaction of Drag, Viewport, or Scene ends when its `can` function turns false, for example when an author withdraws the permission.
- Permissions describe what the widget offers. They do not limit who may edit the document.

### Settings

Settings turns a list of declarations into reflected attributes, entries of the Widget drawer, and bound form controls. Use it for widgets with several settings that the author or the reader changes.

Import `Settings` from `@webwriter/lit/settings`. It is a class mixin: `Settings(LitElementWw, declarations, options?)`. Each setting becomes a reflected reactive property and an entry of `options`. The property types follow the declarations. A `select` is a union of its choices. The mixin options are `entryTimeout`, `negativeBooleans`, and `messages`. The instance has `settingsCore`, whose `set(name, value)` writes a setting as one undo step and whose `labelOf(name, choice?)` gives a label in the widget's language.

| Declaration field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `type` | `String` (default), `Number`, `Boolean`, `"select"`, `"color"`, `"date"`, `"time"`, `"datetime-local"`, `"email"`, `"url"`, `"tel"`, `"password"`, or `"reference"`. Objects and arrays are not settings. |
| `default` | The value while the attribute is absent. It is never written to the document. |
| `label`, `description`, `placeholder` | Text for the drawer. Each may be a [function of the widget](#texts-from-the-widgets-catalog). |
| `group` | An ID from `static optionGroups`. |
| `min`, `max`, `step`, `steps` | Limits of a number. A value outside is moved to the nearest limit, or onto the nearest of `steps`. |
| `options`, `multiple` | The choices of a `select`. Nest choices in `children`. With `multiple` the value is a list. |
| `control` | The drawer control. `"duration"` makes a number a time in seconds that shows as `m:ss`. |
| `unit`, `multiline`, `swatches` | Unit of a number, multi-line text, and suggested colors. |
| `pattern`, `minlength`, `maxlength` | Limits of a text. The module refuses a text that does not fit. |
| `attribute` | The attribute. The default is the name in kebab case, with `no-` in front for a boolean that defaults to true. |
| `disabled` | A function of the widget. It returns true, or the reason as text, to turn the setting off. |

The module also reads `data-ww-setting="name"` on a form control and `data-ww-setting-label="name"` on an element. It fills `data-ww-setting-label` with the label while the template leaves the element empty. Use `"name=value"` for the label of one choice.

```ts
import {LitElementWw} from "@webwriter/lit"
import {Settings} from "@webwriter/lit/settings"
import {html} from "lit"

class WwSimulation extends Settings(LitElementWw, {
  population: {type: Number, default: 200, min: 10, max: 2000, step: 10, label: {_: "Population", de: "Bevölkerung"}},
  speed: {type: Number, default: 1, steps: [0.5, 1, 2], control: "range", label: {_: "Speed"}},
  showChart: {type: Boolean, default: true, label: {_: "Show chart"}},
  mode: {
    type: "select",
    default: "random",
    label: {_: "Movement"},
    options: [{value: "random", label: {_: "Random"}}, {value: "calm", label: {_: "Calm"}}],
    disabled: (widget: {population: number}) => widget.population < 20 && {_: "Needs at least 20 people"},
  },
}) {
  render() {
    return html`
      <p>${this.population} people, speed ${this.speed}, ${this.mode}</p>
      <label><span data-ww-setting-label="population"></span> <input type="number" data-ww-setting="population" /></label>
      <input type="range" data-ww-setting="speed" />
      <label><input type="checkbox" data-ww-setting="showChart" /> Chart</label>
      <select data-ww-setting="mode"></select>
    `
  }
}

customElements.define("ww-simulation", WwSimulation)
```

- A setting is an attribute of the widget. A boolean that defaults to true is stored by the attribute `no-show-chart` and is declared to the drawer with `inverted: true`. `negativeBooleans: "property"` declares it with `attribute: false` instead, for an editor that does not know `inverted`.
- A list is stored as JSON in its attribute. The module never corrects an attribute that it reads. A value that does not fit gives the default.
- Assigning a property reflects the attribute at the next render. `settingsCore.set()` writes it as one undo step and returns false for a value that the setting refuses.
- A bound control shows the value, the limits, and the enabled state. The module sets `min`, `max`, `step`, `pattern`, `minlength`, `maxlength`, `list`, `aria-label`, and `aria-description` where the template has not. It fills an empty `<select>` with the declared choices. A slider over `steps` moves through their positions.
- Entry in a bound control is one undo step. The step ends at the `change` event, when the control loses focus, or after `entryTimeout` milliseconds (default 5000).
- A turned off setting disables its control and its drawer entry. Code can still write it.
- A bound control that sits inside an element with `data-ww-can` refuses input that a reader may not make. Add [Permissions](#permissions) to hide the control as well.
- A class field named like a setting shadows its property. The module warns in development. It also warns about a `group` that `static optionGroups` does not declare.
- The instance's `options` combine the class's `static options` and one entry per setting.
- `static settings = {…}` on a class that extends `Settings(LitElementWw)` declares the same settings. TypeScript then needs a `declare` for every property.

#### Texts from the widget's catalog

`label`, `description`, and `placeholder` of a setting may be functions of the widget, also those of a choice. The module asks the function whenever it shows the text and gives the editor the answer. Type the parameter by what the function reads. Pass `drawer: true` to [`localizer`](#localization-localizer-widgetmsg) so that the editor reads the texts again when a catalog arrives.

```ts
import type {MsgFn} from "@lit/localize"
import {LitElementWw} from "@webwriter/lit"
import {localizer} from "@webwriter/lit/localize"
import {Settings} from "@webwriter/lit/settings"
import {html} from "lit"

class WwSpeedometer extends Settings(LitElementWw, {
  speed: {
    type: Number,
    default: 1,
    min: 0.5,
    max: 4,
    step: 0.5,
    label: (widget: {msg: MsgFn}) => widget.msg("Speed"),
    description: (widget: {msg: MsgFn}) => widget.msg("How fast the run advances."),
  },
  unit: {
    type: "select",
    default: "kmh",
    label: (widget: {msg: MsgFn}) => widget.msg("Unit"),
    options: [
      {value: "kmh", label: (widget: {msg: MsgFn}) => widget.msg("Kilometers per hour")},
      {value: "mph", label: (widget: {msg: MsgFn}) => widget.msg("Miles per hour")},
    ],
  },
}) {
  localize = localizer(this, {
    sourceLocale: "en",
    targetLocales: ["de"],
    load: locale => import(`./generated/${locale}.js`),
    drawer: true,
  })

  msg = this.localize.msg

  render() {
    return html`<output>${this.speed} ${this.unit}</output>`
  }
}

customElements.define("ww-speedometer", WwSpeedometer)
```

### Shortcuts

Shortcuts runs an action from a key. Use it for keys that belong to the widget, such as Delete in a diagram or the arrow keys of a slideshow.

Import `Shortcuts` from `@webwriter/lit/shortcuts`. The keys are declared on [`static actions`](../domeditor/docs/widgets/reference/options-actions.md#action-declaration). The controller has `keysOf(action)`, `labelsOf(action)`, and `running`. `labelsOf` returns the keys as a person reads them on this platform and in the widget's language, such as `⌘D` or `Ctrl+D`. The options are `rendered`, `apple`, and `messages`.

| Declaration | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `shortcut` | On an action. A key such as `"Delete"`, `"Space"`, or `"Mod+D"`, or a list of keys. `Mod` is ⌘ on Apple devices and Ctrl elsewhere. Names are those of `KeyboardEvent.key`. `Space` and `Plus` stand for the characters. A key that also runs while the reader types in a text field is written as an object, `{key: "Mod+Enter", inText: true}`. See [Keys in text fields](#keys-in-text-fields). |
| `can` | On an action. The permission that allows the key for a reader. `"edit"` keeps the key to authors. Without it the key works for readers too. |
| `data-ww-shortcut="action"` | On a button in the shadow template. The module sets its `aria-keyshortcuts`. |
| `data-ww-shortcuts="off"` | On an element. Every key inside is left alone, for a part with its own keymap. |
| `data-ww-shortcuts="on"` | On a component with a closed shadow root. It says that the component holds no text entry, so the keys work while it has focus. |

A key runs the method of the same name on the widget, as the drawer does. A method that returns `false` declines the key.

```ts
import {LitElementWw} from "@webwriter/lit"
import {Shortcuts} from "@webwriter/lit/shortcuts"
import {html} from "lit"

class WwItemList extends LitElementWw {
  static properties = {
    allowRemoving: {type: Boolean, attribute: "allow-removing", reflect: true},
    selected: {state: true},
  }

  static permissions = {
    allowRemoving: {label: {_: "Learners may remove items in this widget"}},
  }

  static actions = {
    remove: {label: {_: "Remove item"}, shortcut: ["Delete", "Backspace"], can: "allowRemoving"},
    clear: {label: {_: "Clear selection"}, shortcut: "Escape", hidden: true},
  }

  declare allowRemoving: boolean
  declare selected: Element | undefined

  #shortcuts = new Shortcuts(this)

  remove() {
    if (!this.selected) return false
    this.selected.remove()
    this.selected = undefined
  }

  clear() {
    if (!this.selected) return false
    this.selected = undefined
  }

  render() {
    return html`
      <div tabindex="0" @click=${(event: Event) => (this.selected = (event.target as Element).closest("li") ?? undefined)}>
        <slot></slot>
      </div>
      <button data-ww-shortcut="remove" ?disabled=${!this.selected} @click=${this.remove}>Remove</button>
      <small>${this.#shortcuts.labelsOf("remove").join(" / ")}</small>
    `
  }
}

customElements.define("ww-item-list", WwItemList)
```

- The module handles a key only when it comes from inside the widget, or from anywhere while the widget is fullscreen. It attaches nothing to `window`.
- Give the widget something focusable, such as a stage with `tabindex="0"`. A click on a canvas leaves the focus on the page, and the keys never arrive. When an action declares a key, the widget warns once in development if its template holds nothing that can take the focus: a `tabindex`, a control, an editable region, or a custom element, which may hold a focusable part. The check runs after the first render that puts something other than styles into the shadow root, so a widget that renders its stage later is not reported for the renders before it.
- A key that belongs to something else is left alone: text entry, an element with a text role, an editable region of the widget, a caret in the authored children, and a key that the focused control uses itself, such as Space on a button or an arrow on a slider. The module ignores keys during text composition.
- Letters ignore case and modifiers must match exactly. A shortcut on a letter or digit also matches the key at its position on a Latin keyboard, when the key produces a letter of another script or when the combination has Alt and the key produces no Latin letter or digit.
- The editor keeps `Mod+Z`, `Mod+Shift+Z`, `Mod+Y`, and `Mod+S`. The module ignores them and warns in development.
- Keys in text fields: see [Keys in text fields](#keys-in-text-fields).
- An action with `disabled: true`, `confirm`, or `input` has no key. A `hidden` action keeps its key, so a navigation key needs no drawer button.
- A method that returns `false` had nothing to do, such as Escape with nothing to cancel. The key goes to the next action that declares it, and to the page when none takes it. Any other result, also `undefined` and a promise, takes the key.
- The method runs as one undo step. The step ends after the next render, or after the returned promise settles and the widget has rendered. A second press of the key does not start the action again while its promise is pending.
- An action whose permission is not granted does nothing.

#### Keys in text fields

Keys typed in a text field are the field's: in a `<textarea>`, an `<input>` that takes text, an element with the role `textbox`, `searchbox`, `combobox`, or `spinbutton`, and an editable region. A shortcut does not run there. That is right for most keys and leaves a code editor without a Run key. Opt a key in with `inText: true` in the object form of `shortcut`. The list can mix strings and objects.

```ts
static actions = {
  run: {label: {_: "Run"}, shortcut: [{key: "Mod+Enter", inText: true}, "R"]},
  stop: {label: {_: "Stop"}, shortcut: {key: "Escape", inText: true}},
}
```

- `Mod+Enter` runs `run` while the caret is in the code editor. The plain `R` runs it only outside text entry, so typing an R in the editor types an R.
- Use `inText` for a key that types nothing: a combination with Ctrl, ⌘, or Alt, Escape, or a function key. In development the module warns once for a key that types, such as a letter, Space, Enter, or an arrow without a modifier, and runs it anyway.
- `inText` changes only the text-entry rule. A key still does not run inside an element with `data-ww-shortcuts="off"`, during text composition, or when it is Mod+Z, Mod+Shift+Z, Mod+Y, or Mod+S. A control that uses the key itself, such as Space on a button, keeps it.
- `keysOf()` and `labelsOf()` list the keys of an object entry like any other.

### Drag

Drag lets a reader or an author pick up items and put them on targets. The items can be authored children or elements that the template renders. Use it to reorder, to move between lists, to copy from a palette, to place an item at a point, or to draw a link from an item to a target.

Import `Drag` from `@webwriter/lit/drag`. The module also exports the types `DragCommitDetail`, `DragPickDetail`, `DragEffect`, and `DragViewport`. The controller has `item`, the element being dragged or picked up, and `via`, which is `"pointer"`, `"keyboard"`, `"click"`, or null. The options are `can`, `rendered`, `messages`, `lift`, `duration`, `easing`, and `viewport`. `viewport` takes the `core` of a [Viewport](#viewport) for a target in world coordinates.

| Marker | Goes on | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `data-ww-drag="kind"` | An item, or a `<slot>` | An item of this kind. On a `<slot>` the assigned authored elements are the items. |
| `data-ww-key` | An item | Its identity. The events report it as `key`. |
| `data-ww-drag-handle` | A part of an item | Only this part starts the drag, and only this part gets `touch-action: none`. The rest of the item scrolls by touch. On a `<slot data-ww-drag>` it says that the assigned elements carry their own handle. Make the handle at least 44 × 44 CSS px on a touch screen. |
| `data-ww-drag-via="pointer keyboard click"` | An item or its `<slot>` | The ways the item is picked up. Without it all three work. |
| `data-ww-drag-effect="move\|copy\|link"` | An item or its `<slot>` | `copy` leaves the item where it is. `link` draws a connector from the item to the pointer. The default is `move`. |
| `data-ww-drag-axis="x\|y"` | An item | The item moves along this axis only. |
| `data-ww-drop="kind …"` | A target | The kinds the target accepts. |
| `data-ww-drop-position="index"` | A target | The target also resolves a place among its items. |
| `data-ww-drop-position="point"` | A target | The target resolves a point on its surface. `data-ww-drop-grid="step"` snaps it. |
| `data-ww-drop-space="world"` | A point target that is the window of a canvas viewport | The point is in the viewport's world coordinates, under its pan and zoom, and the grid is in world units. Pass `{viewport: viewport.core}` as the `viewport` option. The view pans while the pointer is held at the edge of the window. See [Dropping into a viewport](#dropping-into-a-viewport). |
| `data-ww-drop-max="n"` | A target | The capacity. `data-ww-drop-full="swap"` accepts an item when the target is full and reports the occupant as `displaced`. |
| `data-ww-drop-linked="key …"` | A target of links | The keys of the items linked to it, so that capacity and swap hold for links too. |
| `data-ww-label` | An item or a target | Its name in announcements. |

| Event | Dispatched on | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `ww-dragpick` | The item | The item was picked up. A handler can remove entries from `detail.candidates`. `preventDefault()` refuses the pick-up. |
| `ww-dragcommit` | The target | The item was dropped. `detail` has `item`, `key`, `kind`, `effect`, `source`, `target`, `displaced`, `index`, `before`, `x`, `y`, and `slot`. `preventDefault()` refuses the drop. |

In `ww-dragcommit`, `index` and `before` are set for an index target and null otherwise. `x` and `y` are set for a point target and null otherwise: the place of the item's top-left corner in the target's own coordinates, the ones that `left` and `top` of an absolutely positioned child use, snapped to `data-ww-drop-grid`. With `data-ww-drop-space="world"` they are world coordinates. `slot` is the name of the target's slot for a slotted item that moves.

Both events are cancelable and bubble. The first example orders authored children and picks them up by pointer and keyboard only, because a click selects them. The children are focusable in the authored markup, such as `<li tabindex="0">`. Drag moves the children itself.

```ts
import {LitElementWw} from "@webwriter/lit"
import {Drag} from "@webwriter/lit/drag"
import {Permissions} from "@webwriter/lit/permissions"
import {html, nothing} from "lit"

class WwSortList extends LitElementWw {
  static properties = {
    allowReordering: {type: Boolean, attribute: "allow-reordering", reflect: true},
  }

  static permissions = {
    allowReordering: {label: {_: "Learners may reorder the items"}},
  }

  declare allowReordering: boolean

  #permissions = new Permissions(this)
  #drag = new Drag(this, {can: () => this.#permissions.can("allowReordering")})

  constructor() {
    super()
    this.allowReordering = false
  }

  render() {
    const kind = this.#permissions.can("allowReordering") ? "item" : nothing
    return html`
      <div data-ww-drop="item" data-ww-drop-position="index">
        <slot data-ww-drag=${kind} data-ww-drag-via="pointer keyboard"></slot>
      </div>
    `
  }
}

customElements.define("ww-sort-list", WwSortList)
```

For items that the template renders, update the widget's state in the `ww-dragcommit` handler. Drag then animates every item from its old place to its new one.

```ts
import {LitElementWw} from "@webwriter/lit"
import {Drag, type DragCommitDetail} from "@webwriter/lit/drag"
import {html} from "lit"
import {repeat} from "lit/directives/repeat.js"

class WwRankList extends LitElementWw {
  static properties = {
    order: {type: Array, reflect: true},
  }

  declare order: string[]

  #drag = new Drag(this)

  constructor() {
    super()
    this.order = ["Mercury", "Venus", "Earth"]
  }

  #commit(event: CustomEvent<DragCommitDetail>) {
    const {key, index} = event.detail
    if (key === undefined || index === null) return
    const order = this.order.filter(name => name !== key)
    order.splice(index, 0, key)
    this.order = order
  }

  render() {
    return html`
      <ol data-ww-drop="planet" data-ww-drop-position="index" @ww-dragcommit=${this.#commit}>
        ${repeat(this.order, name => name, name => html`<li data-ww-drag="planet" data-ww-key=${name}>${name}</li>`)}
      </ol>
    `
  }
}

customElements.define("ww-rank-list", WwRankList)
```

- An item is picked up by a pointer drag, by Space or Enter, or by a click. It is dropped by releasing it on a target, by a click on a target, or by the arrow keys and Enter. Escape, a canceled pointer, and a release outside a target commit nothing.
- An item that leaves out `keyboard` in `data-ww-drag-via` needs another way to be moved without a pointer. The arrow keys step through the places of an index target. In a point target they move the item by the grid step, or by 10 pixels without a grid and 1 pixel with Shift (world units in a target with `data-ww-drop-space="world"`). Tab switches between targets.
- The module asks `can` before a drag starts, while it runs, and before it commits. The module has no edit mode of its own. Pass a function that reads [Permissions](#permissions).
- The commit event and the render after it form one undo step.
- For an authored child that moves, the module puts it before the item at `detail.before`, with `moveBefore()` where the browser has it so that a child widget keeps its state, and writes the target slot's name to the child's `slot` attribute. It writes nothing else to authored elements. A drop on the item's own place is no commit.
- The module adds `tabindex="0"` to a shadow-rendered item that the keyboard can pick up and that has no `tabindex`. It never adds one to an authored child. A child that the keyboard should pick up needs its own `tabindex` or a focusable handle.
- Animations of the move are skipped for a reader who prefers reduced motion.
- The module sets `touch-action: none` only on what starts a drag, and only while `can` holds. Other touches still scroll. An item with a `data-ww-drag-handle` starts only at the handle, so only the handle gets `touch-action: none`. An item without one is a drag from anywhere, and the whole item gets it: a strip of draggable thumbnails that must scroll by touch needs a handle on each thumbnail. See [Pointer and touch input](../domeditor/docs/widgets/guides/focus.md#pointer-and-touch-input).
- The module announces pick-up, target, drop, and cancellation in a live region, in the widget's language. `data-ww-label` supplies the names.
- Style hooks on shadow elements are `data-ww-dragging` (rendered items), `data-ww-drop-candidate`, `data-ww-drop-over`, `[data-ww-drop-marker]` with `part="ww-drop-marker"`, and `[data-ww-drag-connector]` with `part="ww-drag-connector"`.

### Viewport

Viewport zooms and pans one window onto content that is larger than the widget. Use it for a diagram, a map, a floor plan, or a canvas.

Import `Viewport` from `@webwriter/lit/viewport`. The controller has `x`, `y`, `scale`, `min`, `max`, `width`, and `height`. The methods are `zoomBy(factor, about?)`, `zoomTo(scale, about?)`, `panBy(dx, dy)`, `fit(call?)`, `fitted()`, `centerOn(point, scale?, motion?)`, `setView(view, motion?)`, `autoPan(clientX, clientY)`, `autoPanWhile(source)`, `toWorld(clientX, clientY)`, `toClient(worldX, worldY)`, and `contentChanged()`. A world point `w` is drawn at `w * scale + (x, y)` in CSS pixels from the top-left corner of the window. The module also exports the types `ViewportFitCall`, `ViewportFitDetail`, `ViewportFitOptions`, `ViewportFollow`, `ViewportMotion`, `ViewportSnapshot`, `ViewportStart`, `ViewportWheel`, and `WorldBox`.

| Declaration | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `data-ww-viewport` | The window. A widget has one. By default it is a scroll container: panning is its scroll position, and zoom is the CSS `zoom` of its first child. |
| `data-ww-viewport="canvas"` | The window is a surface that the widget draws. A `<canvas data-ww-viewport>` is the same. The module keeps `x`, `y`, and `scale`, and the widget applies them. |
| `data-ww-viewport="external"` | A library owns the view. Pass `adapter` so that the buttons and keys can drive it. |
| `data-ww-viewport-zoom="min max"` | The zoom limits. The default is `0.25 4`. |
| `data-ww-viewport-fit="content\|width\|none"` | What fit shows. The default is `content`. |
| `data-ww-viewport-pan="x\|y"` | Restricts input panning to one axis. |
| `data-ww-viewport-save="name"` | The widget attribute that keeps the view as `x y scale`, the world point in the center of the window and the scale. |
| `data-ww-viewport-controls` | An element that receives four buttons: zoom out, zoom in, the current percent (which resets to 100 %), and fit. |

The attributes in the subsections below refine the wheel, the first view, the fit, and drops. Each of them has an option, and an attribute on the window wins over its option.

The options are `can`, `canSave`, `bounds`, `margin`, `adapter`, `rendered`, `messages`, and the options behind the attributes below: `wheel`, `start`, `resize`, and `fit`. `bounds` returns the extent of the content in world coordinates for the canvas form. Fit shows it, and panning stays within it. `margin` is how far in CSS pixels the content can be panned past each edge of `bounds`.

```ts
import {LitElementWw} from "@webwriter/lit"
import {Permissions} from "@webwriter/lit/permissions"
import {Viewport} from "@webwriter/lit/viewport"
import {html} from "lit"

class WwFloorPlan extends LitElementWw {
  static properties = {
    src: {type: String, reflect: true},
    allowPanning: {type: Boolean, attribute: "allow-panning", reflect: true},
  }

  static permissions = {
    allowPanning: {label: {_: "Learners may pan and zoom the plan"}},
  }

  declare src: string
  declare allowPanning: boolean

  #permissions = new Permissions(this)
  #viewport = new Viewport(this, {
    can: () => this.#permissions.can("allowPanning"),
    canSave: () => this.#permissions.editing,
  })

  constructor() {
    super()
    this.src = ""
    this.allowPanning = false
  }

  render() {
    return html`
      <div style="height: 300px" data-ww-viewport data-ww-viewport-zoom="0.5 4" data-ww-viewport-save="view" aria-label="Floor plan">
        <img src=${this.src} width="1200" height="800" alt="" />
      </div>
      <div data-ww-viewport-controls></div>
      <output>${Math.round(this.#viewport.scale * 100)} %</output>
    `
  }
}

customElements.define("ww-floor-plan", WwFloorPlan)
```

- Wheel, drag, pinch, keys, and buttons change the view. `Ctrl` or `⌘` with the wheel zooms. In the scroll form the wheel pans natively. The keys are the arrow keys, `+`, `-`, and `0`. While the window has focus, holding Space turns a drag into panning. The middle button does the same.
- `can` gates input and locks the view when it returns false. The methods of the controller are the widget's own code and always work.
- The view is saved to the `data-ww-viewport-save` attribute after it has been still for 200 ms, as one undo step. A fitted view removes the attribute. The module saves in every mode. Pass `canSave: () => permissions.editing` to save the authors' view only.
- A saved view that changes from outside, through undo or another participant, is shown.
- The module adds `tabindex="0"`, `role="group"`, and an `aria-label` to the window where the template has none. Buttons that can do nothing get `aria-disabled`.
- The scroll form writes its zoom into the module's own style sheet, not into the template.
- The controller renders the widget again when the scale changes, and in the canvas form also when the position or size changes.

The next example is a map in the canvas form. It zooms with the plain wheel, opens on a chosen place, fits with some room around the content, glides to a site on a button, and shows why the view was last fitted. The subsections explain each part.

```ts
import {css, html} from "lit"
import {LitElementWw} from "@webwriter/lit"
import {Viewport, type ViewportFitDetail} from "@webwriter/lit/viewport"

type Site = {id: string; name: string; x: number; y: number}

const SITES: Site[] = [
  {id: "gate", name: "Gate", x: 140, y: 120},
  {id: "hall", name: "Hall", x: 520, y: 360},
  {id: "tower", name: "Tower", x: 980, y: 640},
]
const BOARD = {x: 0, y: 0, width: 1200, height: 800}

class WwSiteMap extends LitElementWw {
  static properties = {
    reason: {state: true},
  }

  static styles = css`
    .board { position: relative; height: 280px; overflow: hidden; border: 1px solid #c8c8c8; background: #f4f4f5; }
    .world { position: absolute; left: 0; top: 0; width: 0; height: 0; transform-origin: 0 0; }
    .site { position: absolute; padding: 2px 8px; border: 1px solid #475569; background: white; white-space: nowrap; }
    [data-ww-viewport-controls] { position: absolute; right: 6px; top: 6px; }
  `

  declare reason: string

  #viewport = new Viewport(this, {
    bounds: () => BOARD,
    wheel: "zoom",
    start: () => ({centre: SITES[0], scale: 1.5}),
    fit: {padding: 24, maxScale: 1},
  })

  constructor() {
    super()
    this.reason = ""
    this.addEventListener("ww-viewportfit", (event: Event) => {
      this.reason = (event as CustomEvent<ViewportFitDetail>).detail.reason
    })
  }

  render() {
    const {x, y, scale} = this.#viewport
    return html`
      <div class="board" data-ww-viewport="canvas" data-ww-viewport-zoom="0.25 4" aria-label="Site map">
        <div class="world" style="transform: translate(${x}px, ${y}px) scale(${scale})">
          ${SITES.map(site => html`<span class="site" style="left: ${site.x}px; top: ${site.y}px">${site.name}</span>`)}
        </div>
        <span data-ww-viewport-controls></span>
      </div>
      ${SITES.map(site => html`<button @click=${() => this.#viewport.centerOn(site, 2, {animate: true})}>${site.name}</button>`)}
      <button @click=${() => this.#viewport.fit({animate: true})}>Whole map</button>
      <output>${this.reason}</output>
    `
  }
}

customElements.define("ww-site-map", WwSiteMap)
```

#### Wheel

`data-ww-viewport-wheel` (option `wheel`) says what the plain wheel does over the window. `Ctrl` or `⌘` with the wheel and a pinch on a trackpad zoom in every mode.

| Value | The plain wheel |
|---|---|
| `pan` | Pans. This is the default. |
| `zoom` | Zooms about the pointer. A sideways wheel (one with only `deltaX`) still pans. |
| `page` | Is left to the page, so that the page scrolls over the window. This applies to the canvas form. A scroll container scrolls natively anyway. |

At the limit of the view a panning wheel goes on to the page. Use `zoom` for a surface that fills the screen, such as a diagram editor, and `page` for a window that sits inside a longer page.

#### Start view and centering

The first view of a window is applied once, when the window first has a size. The order is a view carried over from a replaced window, the saved view, the start view, and then the fit. A saved view always wins over the start view.

`data-ww-viewport-start` takes `fit` or `x y scale`. The numbers are the world point in the center of the window and the scale, as in `data-ww-viewport-save`. The scale is optional and defaults to 1. The option `start` takes a value or a function that the module asks once.

| `start` value | First view |
|---|---|
| `"fit"` | The fitted view, as if there were no start view. |
| `{centre, scale?}` | A world point in the center of the window. |
| `{x, y, scale?}` | The position of the world's origin, in CSS pixels from the corner of the window. |
| `{box}` | A box of the world, fitted once. The view stays there until something changes it. |

`centerOn(point, scale?, motion?)` puts a world point in the center of the window and optionally sets the scale. `setView({x, y, scale?})` sets where the world's origin is drawn, and `setView({scale})` sets the scale about the center. Both return a promise that resolves when the view is there. `{animate: true}` glides for 350 ms, and a number is the duration in milliseconds. The animation never runs for a reader who prefers reduced motion, and any other change of the view ends it, which also settles the promise. A call before the window has a size is applied when the window opens. After either call the view is no longer a fitted view.

#### Fitting

A fit shows the content in the window. The content is the box that `fit.target` returns, or else the box that `bounds` returns, in the canvas form, and the first child of the window in the scroll form. A view counts as fitted from its first view, when there is no saved or start view, and after `fit()`, the fit button, and the `0` key. It stays fitted until something else changes it: a zoom, a pan, `zoomTo`, `zoomBy`, `panBy`, `setView`, `centerOn`, or a start or saved view.

| Attribute | Option `fit` | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `data-ww-viewport-fit-padding="px"` | `padding` | Room kept free around the content (canvas form). |
| `data-ww-viewport-fit-max="scale"` | `maxScale` | The largest scale a fit chooses, so that small content is not enlarged. |
| `data-ww-viewport-fit-inset="top right bottom left"` | `inset` | A part of the window that something else covers, such as a drawer. One to four numbers, as CSS margins. The option takes a number or `{top, right, bottom, left}` (canvas form). |
| `data-ww-viewport-follow="all\|window\|none"` | `follow` | When a fitted view fits again by itself. |
| | `target` | A function that returns the box to fit instead of `bounds`, such as the gates instead of the whole board. The fit button and the `0` key use it too (canvas form). |

`fit` may also be a function, which the module asks at every fit.

`follow` takes these values.

- `all` (the default) fits again when the window or the content changes size.
- `window` fits again only when the window changes size.
- `none` never fits again: the view is fitted once and then left alone.

A view that is not fitted keeps its place when the window resizes. `data-ww-viewport-resize="offset|centre"` (option `resize`) says what stays still: the screen offset of the world (the default), or the world point in the center of the window.

`fit(call?)` returns a promise with the snapshot of the view (`x`, `y`, `scale`, `min`, `max`, `width`, `height`). The call takes `animate`, which works as for `centerOn()` and applies to the canvas form only, a `follow` for this fit alone, and `box`, a box of the world to fit instead of the content (canvas form). `fit({follow: "none"})` fits once and leaves the view alone, and `fit({box})` does the same for a chosen box. In the external form the library fits and ignores the options.

`fitted()` returns a promise that resolves when the view is a fitted one that is up to date: at once if it is, and otherwise after the next fit. It rejects with an `AbortError` when the widget disconnects first. Await it before code that needs the view, such as a first measurement.

After every fit the host dispatches `ww-viewportfit`. Its `detail` is the snapshot and a `reason`: `open` for the first view, `request` for `fit()`, the fit button, or the `0` key, and `follow` for a fit that the module made because the window or the content changed size.

#### Panning at the edge

`autoPan(clientX, clientY)` is one step of panning for a pointer in a band at the edge of the window. The band is 64 pixels wide, or a quarter of the window when that is smaller. The view moves towards what lies beyond, up to 16 pixels per call and faster the closer the pointer is to the edge. The method returns whether the view moved, does nothing for a pointer outside the window, and stops at the limits of the view.

Call it once per animation frame during a drag that began elsewhere. `autoPanWhile(source)` does that for you until the gesture ends. `source` is any object with `last.clientX`, `last.clientY`, and an `ended` abort signal, such as a `PointerGesture` from `@webwriter/widget/gesture`. [Drag](#drag) calls `autoPan` by itself for a target in world coordinates.

#### Dropping into a viewport

A drag that ends on the window of a canvas viewport gives the point in the world, under the pan and zoom of the view. Mark the window as a point target in world coordinates with `data-ww-drop-space="world"` and pass the viewport's `core` as the `viewport` option of [Drag](#drag).

```html
<div data-ww-viewport="canvas" data-ww-drop="chip" data-ww-drop-position="point" data-ww-drop-space="world" data-ww-drop-grid="20"></div>
```

`ww-dragcommit` then reports `x` and `y` as the world point under the top-left corner of the lifted item. `data-ww-drop-grid` is in world units. The arrow keys move a keyboard drop by one grid cell, or by 10 world units without a grid and 1 with Shift. The view pans while the pointer is held at the edge of the window. Without the `viewport` option the target is measured as an ordinary point target, and the widget warns in development.

The example takes a chip from a sidebar and places it on the board. The sidebar can cover the left side of the window, so the fit leaves that part free with `data-ww-viewport-fit-inset`.

```ts
import {css, html} from "lit"
import {repeat} from "lit/directives/repeat.js"
import {LitElementWw} from "@webwriter/lit"
import {Drag, type DragCommitDetail} from "@webwriter/lit/drag"
import {Viewport} from "@webwriter/lit/viewport"

type Chip = {id: string; x: number; y: number}

class WwChipBoard extends LitElementWw {
  static properties = {
    chips: {state: true},
    drawer: {type: Boolean},
  }

  static styles = css`
    :host { display: flex; height: 260px; }
    .side { width: 100px; padding: 6px; border: 1px solid #c8c8c8; }
    .source { padding: 4px; border: 1px solid #555; background: white; cursor: grab; touch-action: none; }
    .board { position: relative; flex: 1; min-width: 0; overflow: hidden; border: 1px solid #c8c8c8; background: #f4f4f5; }
    .world { position: absolute; left: 0; top: 0; width: 0; height: 0; transform-origin: 0 0; }
    .chip { position: absolute; width: 60px; height: 30px; box-sizing: border-box; border: 1px solid #555; background: #bfdbfe; }
    [data-ww-drop-over] { background-color: #e0f2fe; }
  `

  declare chips: Chip[]
  declare drawer: boolean

  #viewport = new Viewport(this, {bounds: () => ({x: 0, y: 0, width: 1200, height: 800})})
  #drag = new Drag(this, {viewport: this.#viewport.core})

  constructor() {
    super()
    this.chips = []
    this.drawer = false
  }

  #drop(event: CustomEvent<DragCommitDetail>) {
    const {x, y} = event.detail
    if (x === null || y === null) return
    this.chips = [...this.chips, {id: `chip-${this.chips.length}`, x, y}]
  }

  render() {
    const {x, y, scale} = this.#viewport
    return html`
      <div class="side">
        <div class="source" data-ww-drag="chip" data-ww-drag-effect="copy" data-ww-key="and" data-ww-label="AND gate" tabindex="0">AND</div>
      </div>
      <div
        class="board"
        data-ww-viewport="canvas"
        data-ww-viewport-fit-inset=${this.drawer ? "0 0 0 100" : "0"}
        data-ww-drop="chip"
        data-ww-drop-position="point"
        data-ww-drop-space="world"
        data-ww-drop-grid="20"
        aria-label="Board"
        @ww-dragcommit=${this.#drop}
      >
        <div class="world" style="transform: translate(${x}px, ${y}px) scale(${scale})">
          ${repeat(this.chips, chip => chip.id, chip => html`<div class="chip" style="left: ${chip.x}px; top: ${chip.y}px"></div>`)}
        </div>
        <span data-ww-viewport-controls></span>
      </div>
    `
  }
}

customElements.define("ww-chip-board", WwChipBoard)
```

### Help

Help shows an overlay with one label for each marked control. Use it for a toolbar or a tool with controls that a reader may not recognize.

Import `Help` from `@webwriter/lit/help`. The controller has `open`, `form`, `toggle(force?)`, and `close()`. `form` is `"labels"`, or `"list"` when the widget is too small for labels, and null while the overlay is closed. The options are `anchor` and `messages`. `anchor` selects CSS anchor positioning for the labels. The default is whether the browser supports it.

| Declaration | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `data-ww-help="text"` | On a control or region. The label text. Write it in the widget's language. |
| `data-ww-help-toggle` | On the button that opens and closes the overlay. |
| `data-ww-help-order="n"` | On a marked element. Elements with a number come first, in ascending order, then the others in template order. |
| `data-ww-help-side="top\|bottom\|left\|right"` | On a marked element. The side where the label is tried first. |

```ts
import {LitElementWw} from "@webwriter/lit"
import {Help} from "@webwriter/lit/help"
import {html} from "lit"

class WwToolbar extends LitElementWw {
  #help = new Help(this)

  render() {
    return html`
      <button data-ww-help="Add a node" data-ww-help-order="1">Add</button>
      <button data-ww-help="Remove the selected node" data-ww-help-order="2">Remove</button>
      <div tabindex="0" data-ww-help="The diagram. Use the arrow keys to move the selection."><slot></slot></div>
      <button data-ww-help-toggle aria-label="Help">?</button>
      ${this.#help.open ? html`<small>Press Escape to close the help.</small>` : null}
    `
  }
}

customElements.define("ww-toolbar", WwToolbar)
```

- The overlay shows a label for each marked element that is rendered, visible, and inside the widget. An element with empty text gets none.
- The module appends the overlay to the widget's shadow root, builds it from the live template, and keeps nothing of it between layouts. It exists only while the overlay is open. Its style sheet makes the host a positioning context with `position: relative`.
- While the overlay is open, `aria-describedby` on each element points to its label. For a custom element the same label also describes the control inside its open shadow tree. The module also sets `aria-pressed` on the toggle. These are the only writes to the template.
- While the overlay is open, the module compares the rectangles of the marked elements once per animation frame and lays the labels out again when one moved.
- Escape closes the overlay from anywhere on the page. A click on the overlay closes it. Focus returns to the toggle unless the reader has moved it elsewhere.

### Scene

Scene draws a description of nodes, shapes, paths, text, and images, and reports what the reader does with it. Use it for diagrams, graphs, and circuits where items can be selected, moved, resized, and wired.

Import `SceneController` from `@webwriter/lit/scene`, and `sceneElements` and the event types from `@webwriter/widget/scene`. Register the elements in the widget's scoped registry with `static scopedElements = {...sceneElements}`. For WebGL rendering, register `PixiScene` from `@webwriter/widget/scene/pixi` as `ww-scene`. Only this import bundles `pixi.js`. Use `webglAvailable()` from `@webwriter/widget/scene` to select the renderer.

The controller has `marquee`, `extent()`, `measureText(text, source?)`, `ready`, `toScene(clientX, clientY)`, `toClient(x, y)`, `itemAt(point, {client}?)`, `itemsAt(point, {client}?)`, `endsOf(path)`, `wiresAt(reference)`, `toSVG(options?)`, `toImage(options?)`, `printing`, `restyle()`, and `remeasure()`. `extent()`, `measureText()`, `toSVG()`, and `toImage()` answer for the widget's first `ww-scene`. The options are `can`, `viewport`, `rendered`, `messages`, and `undoHost`.

`can` is a function `(action, item, port?)` or a map from an action to a permission name, such as `{move: "allowMoving"}`. The actions are `select`, `move`, `resize`, and `connect`. For a connection that starts or ends at a port, a function also gets the port element, so that it can refuse one port and not the whole node. `viewport` takes the `core` of a [Viewport](#viewport) for a scene that is the window of a canvas viewport. `undoHost` is the element on which a commit opens its undo step. The editor takes a step only from an event that starts on the widget itself, so a controller in a component inside the widget passes `"outermost"` (the host at the top of the shadow roots above the scene), the widget, or a function that returns it. Without it the step starts on the host of the scene's shadow root.

| Element | Attributes | Draws |
|---|---|---|
| `ww-scene` | `select="none\|single\|multiple"`, `grid`, `move-step`, `connect-click`, `background="dots\|lines"`, `background-spacing` | The scene. `grid` snaps moves and resizes to its multiples. `move-step` is how far an arrow key moves an item (five times as far with Shift). Without it the step is the grid, or 1 and 10 without a grid. `connect-click` lets a click on a port pick a wire up. `background` draws a grid below everything that follows the view. |
| `ww-node` | `x`, `y`, `width`, `height`, `resizable`, `keep-ratio`, `outline="rect\|rounded\|circle\|ellipse"`, `radius` | The HTML content of the node at a scene position. `outline` is the shape where a path ends at the whole node. The selection outline follows it. |
| `ww-group` | `x`, `y`, `scale`, `frame`, `padding`, `label`, `radius` | Its children, moved and scaled together. With `frame` it is also drawn as a box around its members. |
| `ww-shape` | `kind="rect\|circle\|polygon"`, `x`, `y`, `width`, `height`, `r`, `points`, `radius`, `rotate`, `resizable` | A shape. A circle is placed by its center. `radius` rounds the corners of a rect. `rotate` turns a rect about its center and a polygon about `x`, `y`. A rect that is `resizable` has handles while it is selected. |
| `ww-path` | `from`, `to`, `route="straight\|step\|curve\|arc\|orthogonal"`, `bend`, `loop`, `waypoints`, `marker-start`, `marker-end`, `hit-width`, `rewire` | A line between two ends, each written `node:port` or `node`. A path without `from` and `to` follows its `points` property, relative to its `x` and `y`. |
| `ww-text` | `x`, `y`, `rotate`; as a label also `at`, `along`, `side`, `gap`, `follow` | Its text content. Inside a `ww-path` it is a label of the path. |
| `ww-image` | `x`, `y`, `width`, `height`, `href`, `resizable` | A picture. The `source` property takes an image source such as a canvas. |
| `ww-sprites` | `texture` | A batch of sprites from its `items` property. Pixi renderer only. |

Every element also takes `data-ww-key`, `selected`, `selectable`, `movable`, and `aria-label`, and the [constraints](#constraints) below. A path refers to a node by its key, and the events report keys. Style drawn elements with CSS: they take `stroke`, `fill`, and the font properties from their computed style. `--ww-scene-selection` sets the color of the selection outline and of the handles. A port is an element with `data-ww-port="name"` inside a node. `data-ww-link="kind"` on a port starts a wire. `data-ww-accept="kind …"` on a port accepts wires of these kinds. `data-ww-side="left|right|top|bottom"` sets the side where a path leaves a port. Without it the port faces the nearest edge of its node.

| Event | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ww-select` | The reader asks for a selection. `detail.keys` and `detail.items`. |
| `ww-move` | The reader moved items. `detail.items` has the key and the new `x` and `y` of each item. `detail.dx` and `detail.dy` give the movement of the lead item. `detail.pointer` is where the pointer was, or null for a move by keyboard. |
| `ww-moving` | A step of a move, and once more when it is over. It informs, writes nothing, and cannot be canceled. `detail` is that of `ww-move` with `state` (`move` or `end`) and `committed`. |
| `ww-resize` | The reader resized a node, or a rect or an image that is `resizable`. `detail` has `key`, `item`, `x`, `y`, `width`, and `height`. |
| `ww-resizing` | A step of a resize, and once more when it is over. It is to a resize what `ww-moving` is to a move, with `state` `resize` or `end`. |
| `ww-connect` | The reader connected two ports, or two whole nodes. `detail` has `from`, `to` (`node:port`, or `node`), `kind`, `source`, `target`, and `pointer`. |
| `ww-reconnect` | The reader took an end of a wire to another port. `detail` has `path`, `end`, the new `from` and `to`, `previous`, `kind`, `source`, `target`, and `pointer`. |
| `ww-disconnect` | The reader let an end of a wire go where no port is. `detail` has `path`, `end`, `from`, `to`, `kind`, and `pointer`. |
| `ww-connecting` | A wire is held. `detail` says which port it is over. |
| `ww-activate` | A click, a double click, or Enter or Space on an item, also on one that is selected already. |
| `ww-context` | A context menu, the menu key, or a long press by touch, on an item or on the background. |
| `ww-background` | A click, a double click, or a long press on the background. |
| `ww-ready` | The first layout has settled. |
| `ww-sceneerror` | The scene cannot draw something. `detail.code` is `load`, `unsupported`, or `webgl`. |

All events bubble out of the widget's shadow root. `pointer` is `{x, y, clientX, clientY}`: the scene point and the client point.

```ts
import {css, html} from "lit"
import {LitElementWw} from "@webwriter/lit"
import {SceneController} from "@webwriter/lit/scene"
import {sceneElements, type MoveDetail, type SelectDetail} from "@webwriter/widget/scene"

type Box = {id: string; x: number; y: number}

class WwBoxes extends LitElementWw {
  static scopedElements = {...sceneElements}

  static properties = {
    boxes: {type: Array, reflect: true},
    allowMoving: {type: Boolean, attribute: "allow-moving", reflect: true},
    selection: {state: true},
  }

  static permissions = {
    allowMoving: {label: {_: "Learners may move the boxes"}},
  }

  static styles = css`
    ww-scene { height: 240px; border: 1px solid #c8c8c8; }
    ww-node { padding: 8px 14px; background: white; border: 1px solid #6b7280; }
    ww-path { stroke: #6b7280; stroke-width: 2px; }
  `

  declare boxes: Box[]
  declare allowMoving: boolean
  declare selection: string[]

  #scene = new SceneController(this, {can: {move: "allowMoving"}})

  constructor() {
    super()
    this.boxes = [{id: "a", x: 20, y: 20}, {id: "b", x: 200, y: 120}]
    this.allowMoving = false
    this.selection = []
  }

  #select(event: CustomEvent<SelectDetail>) {
    this.selection = event.detail.keys
  }

  #move(event: CustomEvent<MoveDetail>) {
    const moved = new Map(event.detail.items.map(item => [item.key, item]))
    this.boxes = this.boxes.map(box => {
      const to = moved.get(box.id)
      return to ? {...box, x: to.x, y: to.y} : box
    })
  }

  render() {
    return html`
      <ww-scene select="single" grid="10" @ww-select=${this.#select} @ww-move=${this.#move}>
        <ww-path from="a" to="b" route="curve"></ww-path>
        ${this.boxes.map(
          box => html`
            <ww-node data-ww-key=${box.id} x=${box.x} y=${box.y} selectable movable ?selected=${this.selection.includes(box.id)}>
              Box ${box.id}
            </ww-node>
          `,
        )}
      </ww-scene>
    `
  }
}

customElements.define("ww-boxes", WwBoxes)
```

- The scene changes no document. Each interaction previews and then ends in one cancelable event that bubbles. The widget applies the change to its model. The event and the render after it form one undo step. `preventDefault()` refuses the change.
- The selection is the widget's. The scene reads the `selected` attribute and asks for a change with `ww-select`.
- The module asks `can` before a selection, move, resize, or connection, during it, and before it commits. An interaction ends when the answer turns false.
- Pointer, touch, and keyboard all work. A node that is `selectable` or `movable` takes focus. Arrow keys move the selection and commit after a short rest. Moves and wires are announced in a live region.
- The undo step of a commit is opened on the host of the scene's shadow root. For a scene in a component inside the widget use the option `undoHost`.
- The scene writes no position or size to its elements. A preview is a Web Animation that ends with the interaction. A `selectable` or `movable` node without a `tabindex` gets `tabindex="0"`. A port that starts a wire gets `tabindex`, `role="button"`, and an `aria-label` where the template sets none, while the reader may connect, and loses them again.
- Drawn elements and `ww-scene` have custom states for CSS: `:state(hover)` on a drawn item, `:state(failed)` on an image that did not load, `:state(rewiring)` on a path whose end is held, and `:state(wiring)` and `:state(marquee)` on the scene. `ww-scene::part(link)` is the pending wire, `ww-scene::part(resize)` the handles of a rect or image, and `ww-node::part(handle)` the handles of a node.
- A scene inside a scrolling `data-ww-viewport` is zoomed from outside. Pass `viewport` only for the canvas form.
- Call `restyle()` after a style change that no observer sees, and `remeasure()` when ports moved without a change of the document. A change of theme is no such change: see [Theme and zoom](#theme-and-zoom).

#### Theme and zoom

**The theme.** A scene reads computed styles when it draws, and the browser reports no change of a computed style. The scene reads its styles again, and measures its ports, after these changes: a class, a style, or `data-theme` on the widget, on the page's root or body, or on an element between them; a change of `prefers-color-scheme`; and the event `ww-themechange`, which the editor sends on the document after the document theme changed (another bundled theme, a stylesheet of the head, or theme properties on the root or the body). A widget needs no `restyle()` for a theme. Style a scene with the [theme tokens](../domeditor/docs/widgets/guides/theming.md#document-theme-properties-and-fallback-values), such as `stroke: var(--ww-border-color)`, and it follows the theme. An exported page has no editor and sends no event.

**Controls that keep their size.** A node is scaled with the view, so a button in it is half the size at half the zoom. Mark a control with `data-ww-control` and the scene draws it larger by the inverse of the zoom while the view is zoomed out, so that it keeps the size it has at 100 %. Design the control for the [target sizes](../domeditor/docs/widgets/guides/focus.md#target-sizes), 24 px at least and 44 px for a primary control on a touch screen.

```ts
html`<ww-node data-ww-key=${id} x=${x} y=${y} selectable movable>
  ${label}
  <button type="button" data-ww-control aria-label="Remove ${label}" @click=${() => this.remove(id)}>×</button>
</ww-node>`
```

- The scene writes two custom properties on its layer, which every node inherits: `--ww-scene-zoom` (the zoom of the view) and `--ww-scene-counter` (1 divided by it). A rule of the scene, with no specificity, gives `[data-ww-control]` a `scale` of `--ww-scene-counter` where that is greater than 1, up to `--ww-control-limit` (6 by default), and `transform-origin: var(--ww-control-origin, center)`. A rule of the widget on the same element wins, so the widget can write its own `scale` from the two properties.
- A control is larger than its box in the layout, so it can cover its neighbors at a small zoom. Put it at a corner of the node, set `--ww-control-origin` to that corner (for example `top right`), and keep the label out of the way.
- Zooming in scales the control with the node, as everything else. A group's own `scale` is not part of it. The counter applies to the view that the scene itself applies, the canvas form with the `viewport` option. A scene in a scrolling `data-ww-viewport` is zoomed from outside, and its controls scale with the world.
- The scene adopts this rule as a constructed stylesheet into the shadow root, or the document, that holds the scene, and takes it away when the last scene there is gone. It writes nothing into the DOM.
- The resize handles that the scene draws on a selected rect or image are 8 px at every zoom.

#### Paths, markers, and labels

A path ends at a port (`from="a:out"`) or at a whole node (`from="a"`). A node that declares an `outline` is met on that outline, and a node without an `outline` is met at its center. An attached path follows its nodes while they are dragged, moved by keyboard, or resized, and follows the nodes of a group that moves. A path without `from` and `to` is drawn along its `points` property instead.

| Attribute of a `ww-path` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `route` | `straight` (the default), `step`, `curve`, `arc`, or `orthogonal`. `step` and `curve` leave a whole node on the side that faces the other end. |
| `bend` | A number. The path becomes an arc. The control point of the arc is `bend` times the length of the line between the ends away from its middle, to the left of the way from start to end when `bend` is positive. Two paths between the same nodes, one each way, with the same `bend` stay apart. `route="arc"` without `bend` has 0.25, and `bend="0"` is a line. |
| `loop` | An angle in degrees, 0 up and clockwise. A path from a node to itself becomes a loop that leaves and returns where the outline of the node lets it out. An empty value is 45. |
| `waypoints` | The widget's own route: `x,y` pairs, each from the start end, or from the end with `e:` in front, as in `waypoints="20,0 20,-60 e:-20,-60 e:-20,0"`. The route follows its nodes because the points are relative to the ends. |
| `marker-start`, `marker-end` | `none`, `arrow`, `open-arrow`, `triangle`, `triangle-filled`, `diamond`, `diamond-filled`, `circle`, or `circle-open`. |
| `hit-width` | The width, in pixels, of the band in which the path takes the pointer. The default is 12. |
| `rewire` | Lets the reader take an end to another port. See [Wires](#wires). |

`route="orthogonal"` draws horizontal and vertical segments. Each end leaves at its side. The middle segment runs halfway between the ends if no other node is in the way. Otherwise it runs at the nearest free place beside the nodes in the way, 12 pixels clear, and if there is none, the path goes out, across above or below, and in. The route does not avoid other paths and is laid out again whenever a node moves, so use it for scenes of tens of nodes. For more nodes, compute the route in the widget and pass `waypoints`.

A marker has the stroke color of the path and is 8 pixels plus twice the stroke width long. `--ww-scene-marker-size` sets another length. A hollow marker (`triangle`, `diamond`, and `circle-open`) is filled with `--ww-scene-marker-fill`, which is none by default. The path ends at the base of the marker, and an open arrow ends at its tip. A marker shrinks on a path that is too short for it and is never dashed. Markers and labels take the pointer with their path and are part of its selection outline.

A `ww-text` inside a `ww-path` is a label of the path. A path may have several. A label is drawn with the path, takes the pointer with it, and has no tab stop of its own. Label text is not part of the accessible name of the path, so set `aria-label` on a path whose label matters.

| Attribute of a label | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `at` | `start`, `middle` (the default), `end`, or a fraction between 0 and 1 of the length of the path. |
| `along` | Pixels to move along the line, positive towards the end. |
| `side` | `on` the line (the default), or beside it: `left` or `right` of the way, `above`, or `below`. |
| `gap` | Pixels between the line and the box of the label when it is beside the line. The default is 4. |
| `follow` | Turns the label to the direction of the line, upright. `rotate` sets an angle instead. |

The example draws a small state machine. The states are circles, the two transitions between them are arcs with the same `bend`, and a loop leaves the busy state. Each transition has an arrow and a label. The scene shows a dotted background and a framed group, and sizes each state to its name with `measureText()`.

```ts
import {css, html} from "lit"
import {ifDefined} from "lit/directives/if-defined.js"
import {LitElementWw} from "@webwriter/lit"
import {SceneController} from "@webwriter/lit/scene"
import {sceneElements, type MoveDetail} from "@webwriter/widget/scene"

type State = {id: string; x: number; y: number}
type Transition = {id: string; from: string; to: string; label: string; bend?: number; loop?: number}

class WwStateMachine extends LitElementWw {
  static scopedElements = {...sceneElements}

  static properties = {
    states: {type: Array, reflect: true},
  }

  static styles = css`
    ww-scene { height: 260px; color: #334155; --ww-scene-grid-color: #94a3b8; }
    ww-node { display: grid; place-items: center; box-sizing: border-box; background: white; border: 2px solid #334155; }
    ww-path { stroke: #334155; stroke-width: 2px; }
    ww-path ww-text { fill: #1e293b; font-size: 13px; white-space: pre-line; background-color: white; padding: 0 4px; }
    ww-group { fill: #f1f5f9; stroke: #94a3b8; stroke-dasharray: 4 3; color: #64748b; }
    ww-text.title { fill: #0f172a; font-size: 14px; stroke: white; stroke-width: 3px; }
  `

  declare states: State[]

  #transitions: Transition[] = [
    {id: "go", from: "idle", to: "busy", label: "start", bend: 0.25},
    {id: "back", from: "busy", to: "idle", label: "stop", bend: 0.25},
    {id: "retry", from: "busy", to: "busy", label: "retry\nlater", loop: 45},
  ]

  #scene = new SceneController(this)

  constructor() {
    super()
    this.states = [{id: "idle", x: 40, y: 80}, {id: "busy", x: 260, y: 80}]
  }

  #move(event: CustomEvent<MoveDetail>) {
    const moved = new Map(event.detail.items.map(item => [item.key, item]))
    this.states = this.states.map(state => {
      const to = moved.get(state.id)
      return to ? {...state, x: to.x, y: to.y} : state
    })
  }

  render() {
    return html`
      <ww-scene select="single" background="dots" background-spacing="20" @ww-move=${this.#move}>
        <ww-group frame label="Machine" padding="16">
          ${this.states.map(state => {
            const width = Math.max(64, this.#scene.measureText(state.id, {fontSize: 14}).width + 24)
            return html`
              <ww-node data-ww-key=${state.id} x=${state.x} y=${state.y} width=${width} height="64" outline="circle" selectable movable>${state.id}</ww-node>
            `
          })}
        </ww-group>
        ${this.#transitions.map(
          transition => html`
            <ww-path
              data-ww-key=${transition.id}
              from=${transition.from}
              to=${transition.to}
              bend=${ifDefined(transition.bend)}
              loop=${ifDefined(transition.loop)}
              marker-end="arrow"
              hit-width="24"
            >
              <ww-text side="above" at="middle">${transition.label}</ww-text>
            </ww-path>
          `,
        )}
        <ww-text class="title" x="8" y="8">States: ${this.states.length}</ww-text>
      </ww-scene>
    `
  }
}

customElements.define("ww-state-machine", WwStateMachine)
```

#### Shapes, text, groups, and the background

`ww-shape kind="rect"` takes `radius` for rounded corners. `rotate` (degrees, clockwise) turns a rect about its center, and a polygon and a text about their `x`, `y`.

A `ww-text` is a text of one or more lines at `x`, `y`. The scene reads these properties of its style.

- `white-space: pre-line` (also `pre` and `pre-wrap`) keeps the line breaks of its text. Otherwise line breaks are spaces. `line-height` sets the distance of the lines.
- `text-anchor` (`start`, `middle`, `end`) says which end of the lines is at `x`.
- `dominant-baseline` says what `y` is: the top of the text (the default), its middle (`middle` or `central`), its bottom (`text-after-edge`), or the alphabetic baseline of the first line (`alphabetic`). The Pixi renderer puts that baseline about 0.8 em below the top of the line.
- `stroke` and `stroke-width` make a halo under the letters. `background-color`, `padding`, and `border-radius` make a box behind it. A label of a path has them too.

`measureText(text, source?)` of the controller (and of `ww-scene`) tells the size a text will have before anything is drawn: `{width, height, lines, lineHeight}` in scene pixels, with the widest line and the height of all lines. `source` is an element whose font is used, such as a `ww-text`, or some entries of a font (`{fontSize: 14}`; the other entries are `fontFamily`, `fontWeight`, `fontStyle`, and `lineHeight`). Without a `source` the font of the scene is used. `\n` breaks lines. Use it to size a node to its label. The result is zero until the scene has been connected. `extent()` includes texts with their padding, the markers and labels of paths, rotated outlines, and the frames of groups.

A `ww-group` with `frame` is drawn as a box around its members: nodes, drawn items, and other groups. `padding` is the distance in pixels (8 by default), `radius` rounds the corners, and `label` appears above the box. The box has the `fill`, `stroke`, `stroke-width`, and `stroke-dasharray` of the group and follows its members while they move. An empty group has no box. Where the group is selectable or movable, a press anywhere inside the box moves the group and what it holds.

`background="dots"` or `"lines"` on `ww-scene` draws a grid below everything, with its marks at the multiples of `background-spacing` (or of `grid`, or 20). The grid follows the view, covers the visible part of the scene, and is drawn as one tiled pattern. `--ww-scene-grid-color` and `--ww-scene-grid-size` (the radius of a dot, the width of a line) style it. It takes no pointer and is no part of `extent()`.

#### Reacting while the reader acts

The commit events (`ww-select`, `ww-move`, `ww-resize`, `ww-connect`, `ww-reconnect`, and `ww-disconnect`) are the place to change the model. The other events inform. They write nothing and cannot be canceled, except `ww-connecting` and `ww-context`, which say so.
